claim: Single particle cryo-electron microscopy (cryoEM) is often performed under the assumption that particles are not adsorbed to the air-water interfaces and in thin, vitreous ice.
source: Single particle cryo-electron microscopy (cryoEM) is often performed under the assumption that particles are not adsorbed to the air-water interfaces and in thin, vitreous ice.
evidence: This is a statement about common practice in the field, representing established knowledge about how single particle cryoEM is typically performed.

claim: Fiducial-less tomography was performed on over 50 different cryoEM grid/sample preparations.
source: In this study, we performed fiducial-less tomography on over 50 different cryoEM grid/sample preparations to determine the particle distribution within the ice and the overall geometry of the ice in grid holes.
evidence: This is directly stated in the abstract and supported by the data presented in Tables 1 and 2 showing 46 samples.

claim: Over 1000 tomograms were studied to determine particle distribution.
source: Surprisingly, by studying particles in holes in 3D from over 1000 tomograms, we have determined that the vast majority of particles (approximately 90%) are adsorbed to an air-water interface.
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the abstract and confirmed in the Results section.

claim: Approximately 90% of particles are adsorbed to an air-water interface.
source: Surprisingly, by studying particles in holes in 3D from over 1000 tomograms, we have determined that the vast majority of particles (approximately 90%) are adsorbed to an air-water interface.
evidence: This is the primary finding of the study, supported by systematic analysis of over 1000 tomograms across 50+ samples as documented in Tables 1 and 2.

claim: Particle adsorption to air-water interfaces has potential implications regarding protein denaturation, conformational change, and preferred orientation.
source: The implications of this observation are wide-ranging, with potential ramifications regarding protein denaturation, conformational change, and preferred orientation.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the main finding about particle adsorption, drawing on cross-disciplinary literature about protein behavior at air-water interfaces.

claim: Fiducial-less cryo-electron tomography on single particle grids can be used to determine ice thickness.
source: We also show that fiducial-less cryo-electron tomography on single particle grids may be used to determine ice thickness, optimal single particle collection areas and strategies, particle heterogeneity, and de novo models for template picking and single particle alignment.
evidence: This is demonstrated through the ice thickness measurements presented in Table 1 and Figure 3.

claim: Fiducial-less cryo-electron tomography on single particle grids can be used to determine optimal single particle collection areas and strategies.
source: We also show that fiducial-less cryo-electron tomography on single particle grids may be used to determine ice thickness, optimal single particle collection areas and strategies, particle heterogeneity, and de novo models for template picking and single particle alignment.
evidence: This is demonstrated through examples in the Results section showing how tomography reveals optimal collection locations.

claim: Fiducial-less cryo-electron tomography on single particle grids can be used to assess particle heterogeneity.
source: We also show that fiducial-less cryo-electron tomography on single particle grids may be used to determine ice thickness, optimal single particle collection areas and strategies, particle heterogeneity, and de novo models for template picking and single particle alignment.
evidence: This is demonstrated through examples showing particle behavior and structural variations in the Results section.

claim: Fiducial-less cryo-electron tomography on single particle grids can be used to generate de novo models for template picking and single particle alignment.
source: We also show that fiducial-less cryo-electron tomography on single particle grids may be used to determine ice thickness, optimal single particle collection areas and strategies, particle heterogeneity, and de novo models for template picking and single particle alignment.
evidence: This is demonstrated through the DnaB helicase-helicase loader example in Figure 9 and the corresponding Results section.

claim: An ideal single particle cryoEM grid would have particles 10 nm or farther from the air-water interfaces.
source: An ideal grid and sample for single particle collection would have the majority of areas in holes maximally occupied by non-adsorbed, non-interacting particles 10 nm or farther from the air-water interfaces, particles oriented randomly, vitreous ice thin enough to contain the particles plus about 20 nm of additional space, where none of the particles overlap in the beam direction, and where the beam direction is normal to the areas of interest (Figure 1).
evidence: This is stated as a definition of ideal conditions based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: An ideal single particle cryoEM grid would have particles oriented randomly.
source: An ideal grid and sample for single particle collection would have the majority of areas in holes maximally occupied by non-adsorbed, non-interacting particles 10 nm or farther from the air-water interfaces, particles oriented randomly, vitreous ice thin enough to contain the particles plus about 20 nm of additional space, where none of the particles overlap in the beam direction, and where the beam direction is normal to the areas of interest (Figure 1).
evidence: This is stated as a definition of ideal conditions based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: An ideal single particle cryoEM grid would have vitreous ice thin enough to contain the particles plus about 20 nm of additional space.
source: An ideal grid and sample for single particle collection would have the majority of areas in holes maximally occupied by non-adsorbed, non-interacting particles 10 nm or farther from the air-water interfaces, particles oriented randomly, vitreous ice thin enough to contain the particles plus about 20 nm of additional space, where none of the particles overlap in the beam direction, and where the beam direction is normal to the areas of interest (Figure 1).
evidence: This is stated as a definition of ideal conditions based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Jacques Dubochet et al., 1988 observed issues with regards to air-water interface and particle orientation for a small number of samples.
source: For instance, Jacques Dubochet et al., 1988 observed issues with regards to air-water interface and particle orientation for a small number of samples.
evidence: This is a citation to prior work by Dubochet et al., 1988.

claim: Upon contact with a clean air-water interface, proteins in solution will denature, forming an insoluble, denatured protein film.
source: In a recent review by Robert Glaeser (Glaeser and Han, 2017), evidence (Trurnit, 1960) using Langmuir-Blodgett (LB) troughs (Langmuir, 1917) was used to propose that upon contact with a clean air-water interface, proteins in solution will denature, forming an insoluble, denatured protein film.
evidence: This is cited from Glaeser and Han, 2017, which references Trurnit, 1960.

claim: The denatured protein film reduces the surface tension at the air-water interface.
source: This film reduces the surface tension at the air-water interface and might act as a barrier between the remaining particles in solution and the air.
evidence: This is stated as an inference based on cited literature about protein behavior at air-water interfaces.

claim: The time for a particle with a mass of 100 kDa to 1 MDa to first reach the air-water interface ranges from 1 ms to 0.1 s.
source: Estimates for the amount of time a particle with a mass of 100 kDa to 1 MDa in solution might take to first reach the air-water interface (bulk diffusion) range from 1 ms to 0.1 s (Naydenova and Russo, 2017; Taylor and Glaeser, 2008).
evidence: This is cited from Naydenova and Russo, 2017 and Taylor and Glaeser, 2008.

claim: Proteins commonly adsorb to the air-water interface and form <10 nm thick denatured viscoelastic protein network films.
source: More recent literature, using LB troughs, substantiates that 10–1000 mL volumes of various proteins (commonly 10–1000 kDa and at ≲1 mg/mL) in buffer commonly adsorb to the air-water interface and form <10 nm thick (Gunning et al., 1996; Vliet et al., 2002) denatured viscoelastic protein network films (Birdi, 1972; Damodaran and Song, 1988; de Jongh et al., 2004; Dickinson et al., 1988; Graham and Phillips, 1979; Yano, 2012).
evidence: This is cited from multiple sources in the food science and surface physics literature.

claim: The time for adsorption to begin due to bulk diffusion may be on the order of 0.1 to 1 ms.
source: The time it takes for adsorption to begin due to bulk diffusion may be on the order of 0.1 to 1 ms, depending on the protein (Kudryashova et al., 2005).
evidence: This is cited from Kudryashova et al., 2005.

claim: Surface diffusion time for a protein that denatures at the air-water interface might be on the order of tens of milliseconds.
source: For a protein that denatures at the air-water interface (surface diffusion), the surface diffusion time might be on the order of tens of milliseconds (Kudryashova et al., 2005), depending on factors including protein and concentration, surface hydrophobicity, amount of disordered structure, secondary structure, concentration of intramolecular disulfide bonds, buffer, and temperature.
evidence: This is cited from Kudryashova et al., 2005.

claim: Higher bulk protein concentrations increase the protein network thickness.
source: Higher bulk protein concentrations have been shown to increase the protein network thickness (Meinders et al., 2001).
evidence: This is cited from Meinders et al., 2001.

claim: Adding surfactants to protein solutions in which a protein network film has already formed at the air-water interface will displace the protein layer.
source: It has been shown using atomic force microscopy (AFM) imaging of LB protein films that these protein network films may not completely denature down to individual amino acids: adding surfactants to protein solutions in which a protein network film has already formed at the air-water interface will displace the protein layer (desorption [MacRitchie, 1998]) (Gunning and Morris, 2018; Mackie et al., 1999; Wilde et al., 2004) and the resulting protein network segments might partially re-fold in solution (Gunning and Morris, 2018; Mackie et al., 1999; Morris and Gunning, 2008).
evidence: This is cited from multiple sources studying protein-surfactant interactions at air-water interfaces.

claim: Proteins with β-sheets partially unfold, with the hydrophobic β-sheets remaining in-tact at the air-water interface.
source: Similar experiments using LB troughs have also shown that proteins with β-sheets partially unfold, with the hydrophobic β-sheets remaining in-tact at the air-water interface and with potentially one or more layers of unstructured, but connected, hydrophilic amino acid strands just below the air-water interface (Yano et al., 2009).
evidence: This is cited from Yano et al., 2009.

claim: β-sheets commonly consist of alternating hydrophobic and hydrophilic sidechains.
source: This potential for β-sheets to survive bulk protein denaturation is likely due to β-sheets commonly consisting of alternating hydrophobic and hydrophilic (polar or charged) sidechains (Zhang et al., 1993), with the hydrophobic sidechains orienting towards the air.
evidence: This is cited from Zhang et al., 1993.

claim: The more stable a protein in bulk solution, the more robust the resulting protein network film at the air-water interface.
source: Measurements of shear stress and compressibility of protein network films versus the internal cohesion of the constituent protein show a correlation: the more stable a protein in bulk solution, the more robust the resulting protein network film at the air-water interface (Martin et al., 2005).
evidence: This is cited from Martin et al., 2005.

claim: The fiducial-less tomography pipeline at NYSBC allows for the routine study of grids and samples prepared for single particle cryoEM in three dimensions.
source: The fiducial-less tomography pipeline at the New York Structural Biology Center (NYSBC) consisting of Leginon (Suloway et al., 2005; Suloway et al., 2009) or SerialEM (Mastronarde, 2003) for tilt-series collection and Appion-Protomo (Noble and Stagg, 2015; Winkler and Taylor, 2006) for tilt-series alignment allows for the routine study of grids and samples prepared for single particle cryoEM in three dimensions.
evidence: This is stated as a methodological capability demonstrated through the study's data collection.

claim: Most particles prepared with sample incubation times on the order of 1 s on the grid are within 5–10 nm of an air-water interface.
source: As shown in Table 1, Table 2, Figure 4, and the Videos, most particles prepared with sample incubation times on the order of 1 s on the grid are within 5–10 nm of an air-water interface (ie. are characterized by B2, B3, or B4 in Table 2).
evidence: This is supported by measurements presented in Tables 1 and 2.

claim: The average ice thickness at the center of holes is about 30 ± 13 nm for gold nanowire grids prepared with Spotiton.
source: At the center, the ice thickness is about 30 ± 13 nm for gold nanowire grids prepared with Spotiton (N = 11), 47 ± 40 nm for carbon nanowire grids prepared with Spotiton (N = 17), and 56 ± 35 nm for carbon holey grids prepared using conventional methods (N = 10) (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the tomography data presented in Figure 3A.

claim: The average ice thickness at the center of holes is about 47 ± 40 nm for carbon nanowire grids prepared with Spotiton.
source: At the center, the ice thickness is about 30 ± 13 nm for gold nanowire grids prepared with Spotiton (N = 11), 47 ± 40 nm for carbon nanowire grids prepared with Spotiton (N = 17), and 56 ± 35 nm for carbon holey grids prepared using conventional methods (N = 10) (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the tomography data presented in Figure 3A.

claim: The average ice thickness at the center of holes is about 56 ± 35 nm for carbon holey grids prepared using conventional methods.
source: At the center, the ice thickness is about 30 ± 13 nm for gold nanowire grids prepared with Spotiton (N = 11), 47 ± 40 nm for carbon nanowire grids prepared with Spotiton (N = 17), and 56 ± 35 nm for carbon holey grids prepared using conventional methods (N = 10) (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the tomography data presented in Figure 3A.

claim: Ice thickness about 100 nm from the edge of grid holes is about 61 ± 11 nm for gold nanowire grids prepared with Spotiton.
source: Ice thickness about 100 nm from the edge of grid holes is about 61 ± 11 nm for gold nanowire grids prepared with Spotiton (N = 4), 107 ± 54 nm for carbon nanowire grids prepared with Spotiton (N = 16), and 99 ± 24 nm for carbon holey grids prepared using conventional methods (N = 8) (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the tomography data presented in Figure 3B.

claim: Ice thickness about 100 nm from the edge of grid holes is about 107 ± 54 nm for carbon nanowire grids prepared with Spotiton.
source: Ice thickness about 100 nm from the edge of grid holes is about 61 ± 11 nm for gold nanowire grids prepared with Spotiton (N = 4), 107 ± 54 nm for carbon nanowire grids prepared with Spotiton (N = 16), and 99 ± 24 nm for carbon holey grids prepared using conventional methods (N = 8) (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the tomography data presented in Figure 3B.

claim: Ice thickness about 100 nm from the edge of grid holes is about 99 ± 24 nm for carbon holey grids prepared using conventional methods.
source: Ice thickness about 100 nm from the edge of grid holes is about 61 ± 11 nm for gold nanowire grids prepared with Spotiton (N = 4), 107 ± 54 nm for carbon nanowire grids prepared with Spotiton (N = 16), and 99 ± 24 nm for carbon holey grids prepared using conventional methods (N = 8) (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the tomography data presented in Figure 3B.

claim: The average tilt of particle layers at the centers of holes is 4.7 ± 3.0°.
source: The average tilt ± (one standard deviation and measurement error) of layers at the centers of holes is 4.7 ± 3.0° and at the edges of holes is 6.9 ± 3.5° (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the tomography data presented in Figure 3.

claim: The average tilt of particle layers at the edges of holes is 6.9 ± 3.5°.
source: The average tilt ± (one standard deviation and measurement error) of layers at the centers of holes is 4.7 ± 3.0° and at the edges of holes is 6.9 ± 3.5° (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the tomography data presented in Figure 3.

claim: About 83% of the samples contained single particle layers in the centers of holes.
source: About 83% of the samples contained single particle layers (N = 30) in the centers of holes while about 22% contained double particle layers (N = 8; several samples have different holes with single and double layers of particles in their centers).
evidence: This is calculated from the data presented in Tables 1 and 2.

claim: About 22% of samples contained double particle layers in the centers of holes.
source: About 83% of the samples contained single particle layers (N = 30) in the centers of holes while about 22% contained double particle layers (N = 8; several samples have different holes with single and double layers of particles in their centers).
evidence: This is calculated from the data presented in Tables 1 and 2.

claim: Near the edges of holes, about 7% contain single particle layers.
source: Near the edges of holes, about 7% contain single particle layers (N = 2), while about 75% contained double particle layers (N = 21).
evidence: This is calculated from the data presented in Tables 1 and 2.

claim: Near the edges of holes, about 75% contained double particle layers.
source: Near the edges of holes, about 7% contain single particle layers (N = 2), while about 75% contained double particle layers (N = 21).
evidence: This is calculated from the data presented in Tables 1 and 2.

claim: Several samples show clear protein fragments at air-water interfaces.
source: Several samples show clear protein fragments at air-water interfaces (samples #4–6, 10–14, 26, 30, 34–38, and 46; Figure 6A–E, blue arrows).
evidence: This is observed directly in the tomography data and shown in Figure 6.

claim: Neural receptor densities on the air-water interface show a clear relationship in size to the 13 kDa Ig-like domains that constitute the proteins.
source: For the neural receptors (sample #13), densities on the air-water interface show a clear relationship in size to the 13 kDa Ig-like domains that constitute the proteins.
evidence: This is observed directly in the tomography data for sample #13.

claim: Several apoferritin samples show apparent protein fragments at the air-water interfaces.
source: Several apoferritin samples (samples #34–38) also show apparent protein fragments at the air-water interfaces (Figure 6B and Videos 2–7 corresponding to samples #34–38).
evidence: This is observed directly in the tomography data and shown in Figure 6B and Videos 2-7.

claim: One hemagglutinin sample contained holes where the ice became too thin for whole particles to reside and is instead occupied exclusively by protein fragments.
source: One hemagglutinin sample contained holes where the ice became too thin for whole particles to reside and is instead occupied exclusively by protein fragments (Figure 6C and Video 7 corresponding to sample #4).
evidence: This is observed directly in the tomography data and shown in Figure 6C and Video 7.

claim: GDH shows sequestered protein fragments in open areas near particles at the air-water interface.
source: GDH similarly shows sequestered protein fragments in open areas near particles at the air-water interface (Figure 6E and Video 9 corresponding to sample #30).
evidence: This is observed directly in the tomography data and shown in Figure 6E and Video 9.

claim: Several samples show clear partial particles at air-water interfaces.
source: Several samples show clear partial particles at air-water interfaces (samples 10–14, 34–39, and 46; Figure 6A,B,F, green arrows).
evidence: This is observed directly in the tomography data and shown in Figure 6.

claim: Only two samples exhibit ideal characteristics: less than 100 nm ice thickness, no overlapping particles, little or no preferred orientation, and areas with no particle-air-water interface interaction.
source: Only two samples, #25: protein in nanodisc and #46: protein on streptavidin, exhibit ideal characteristics – less than 100 nm ice thickness, no overlapping particles, little or no preferred orientation, and areas with no particle-air-water interface interaction.
evidence: This is determined from analysis of all samples in Tables 1 and 2.

claim: Air-water interfaces are tilted between 0° and 16° relative to the electron beam when at a nominal stage tilt of 0°.
source: We have found that air-water interfaces are tilted between 0° and 16° relative to the electron beam when at a nominal stage tilt of 0° (Table 2).
evidence: This is measured from the tomography data and presented in Table 2.

claim: The average tilt of particle layers at the centers of holes is 4.8°±3.1°.
source: The average tilt ± (one standard deviation and measurement error) of particle layers at the centers of holes is 4.8°±3.1° (N = 89) and at the edges of holes is 6.9°±3.5° (N = 61) (Table 2, Figure 3, Figure 4).
evidence: This is measured from the tomography data and presented in Table 2 and Figure 3.

claim: The average tilt of particle layers at the edges of holes is 6.9°±3.5°.
source: The average tilt ± (one standard deviation and measurement error) of particle layers at the centers of holes is 4.8°±3.1° (N = 89) and at the edges of holes is 6.9°±3.5° (N = 61) (Table 2, Figure 3, Figure 4).
evidence: This is measured from the tomography data and presented in Table 2 and Figure 3.

claim: A lack of apparent preferred orientation in single particle micrographs does not imply that the particles are not adsorbed to the air-water interfaces.
source: It is important to note that a lack of apparent preferred orientation in single particle micrographs does not imply that the particles are not adsorbed to the air-water interfaces.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that many particles without apparent preferred orientation are still adsorbed to air-water interfaces as shown in the tomography data.

claim: CryoET was used on several HIV-1 trimer preparations with receptors to understand the stoichiometry of the bound receptors by direct visualization of individual particles in 3D.
source: For example, cryoET has been used on several HIV-1 trimer preparations with receptors to understand the stoichiometry of the bound receptors by direct visualization of individual particles in 3D (samples #5–7 corresponding to Videos 8, 13 and 14).
evidence: This is demonstrated through the analysis of samples #5-7.

claim: For the glycoprotein with bound lipids sample, near the edges of the hole the particles with lipids existed in two layers at the air-water interfaces, and beyond a radial distance from the edge of about 300 nm where the ice became about 15 nm thin the particles and lipids dissociated.
source: In another example, sample #17, the size of the 'glycoprotein with bound lipids' particles varied discretely with the radial distance from the edge of holes (Figure 4 and Video 15). In single particle cryoEM micrographs, this observation was not immediately explicable and would have required a single particle data collection followed by alignment and classification before reliable conclusions could be made. Instead, a single tomogram of the sample was collected and it was observed that near the edges of the hole the particles with lipids existed in two layers at the air-water interfaces. Beyond a radial distance from the edge of about 300 nm where the ice became about 15 nm thin the particles and lipids dissociated, with the particles remaining in a single layer (see Video 1 for sample #20).
evidence: This is observed directly in the tomography data for sample #17.

claim: Fiducial-less single particle tomography on DnaB helicase-helicase loader grids was employed to generate a de novo initial model, which was then used both as a template for picking all views of the particle in the single particle micrographs and as an initial model for single particle alignment, resulting in a 4.1 Å isotropic structure.
source: To ameliorate this problem, five tilt-series in representative areas were collected at the end of a single particle collection session, aligned in Appion-Protomo (Noble and Stagg, 2015; Winkler and Taylor, 2006), and about 1000 particles were processed through sub-tomogram alignment, classification, and multireference alignment using Dynamo (Castaño-Díez et al., 2012; Castaño-Díez et al., 2017). This resulted in three de novo initial models, each showing an asymmetric cracked ring (Figure 9B), contradicting the C6-symmetric reconstruction determined by 2D classification and common-lines approaches. The most populated class from single particle tomography (SPT) was then used to both template pick the single particle micrographs in Relion (Scheres, 2012) and as initial models for single particle alignment, resulting in a 4.1 Å structure of the DnaB helicase-helicase loader (manuscript in preparation) (Figure 9B).
evidence: This is demonstrated through the workflow shown in Figure 9 for sample #33.

claim: CryoET revealed that the apparent symmetry in the prevalent top view particles of DnaB helicase-helicase loader as seen in the Gaussian picked 2D class averages was in fact a projection of the globally asymmetric particle.
source: In this example, cryoET revealed that the apparent symmetry in the prevalent top view particles as seen in the Gaussian picked 2D class averages was in fact a projection of the globally asymmetric particle.
evidence: This is demonstrated through the comparison of 2D classification results and tomography-derived models in Figure 9.

claim: Over 1000 single particle tomograms of over 50 different sample preparations have been collected over a 1-year period.
source: Over 1000 single particle tomograms of over 50 different sample preparations have been collected over a 1-year period.
evidence: This is stated as a description of the data collection scope.

claim: 21 of 46 samples (46%) showed regions of ice in grid holes with near-ideal conditions.
source: Samples showing regions of ice in grid holes with near-ideal conditions – less than 100 nm ice thickness, no overlapping particles, and little or no preferred orientation – are highlighted in blue (21 of 46 samples; 46%) in Tables 1 and 2.
evidence: This is calculated from the data presented in Tables 1 and 2.

claim: 2 of 46 samples (4%) showed regions of ice in grid holes with ideal conditions.
source: Samples showing regions of ice in grid holes with ideal conditions – near-ideal conditions plus no particle-air-water interface interaction – are highlighted in green (2 of 46 samples; 4%).
evidence: This is calculated from the data presented in Tables 1 and 2.

claim: Over half of the samples only contained areas that are not ideal for collection due to ice thickness being greater than 100 nm, overlapping particles, and/or preferred orientation.
source: Over half of the samples only contained areas that are not ideal for collection due to ice thickness being greater than 100 nm, overlapping particles, and/or preferred orientation.
evidence: This is inferred from the data presented in Tables 1 and 2.

claim: Most tilt-series were collected using Leginon on the Krios microscopes and the F20, with the remaining collected using SerialEM on the F20.
source: Most tilt-series were collected using Leginon (Suloway et al., 2005; Suloway et al., 2009) on the Krios microscopes and the F20, with the remaining collected using SerialEM (Mastronarde, 2003) on the F20.
evidence: This describes the data collection methods used in the study.

claim: Most tilt-series were collected bi-directionally with a tilt range of −45° to 45° and a tilt increment of 3°.
source: Most tilt-series were collected bi-directionally with a tilt range of −45° to 45° and a tilt increment of 3°.
evidence: This describes the data collection parameters used in the study.

claim: Most tilt-series were collected at a nominal defocus between 4 to 6 microns.
source: Most tilt-series were collected at a nominal defocus between 4 to 6 microns.
evidence: This describes the data collection parameters used in the study.

claim: Most tilt-series were collected with a dose rate around 8 e-/pixel/s and an incident dose between 1.5 and 3.0 e-/Å2 for the zero-degree tilt image, resulting in a total dose between 50 and 150 e-/Å2.
source: Most tilt-series were collected with a dose rate around 8 e-/pixel/s and an incident dose between 1.5 and 3.0 e-/Å2 for the zero-degree tilt image, with increasing dose for higher tilt angles according to the cosine of the tilt angle, resulting in a total dose between 50 and 150 e-/Å2.
evidence: This describes the data collection parameters used in the study.

claim: Most tilt-series were collected at a pixelsize between 1 and 2.2 Å.
source: Most tilt-series were collected at a pixelsize between 1 and 2.2 Å.
evidence: This describes the data collection parameters used in the study.

claim: Each high-magnification tilt-series typically collect in around 15 min.
source: Each high-magnification tilt-series typically collect in around 15 min, while hole magnification tilt-series take about 30 min.
evidence: This describes the time required for data collection.

claim: All tilt-series were aligned using Appion-Protomo.
source: All tilt-series were aligned using Appion-Protomo (Noble and Stagg, 2015).
evidence: This describes the data processing method used in the study.

claim: Tilt-series typically align well in 20–60 min.
source: Tilt-series typically align well in 20–60 min.
evidence: This describes the time required for data processing.

claim: Nearly all tilt-series were alignable.
source: Nearly all tilt-series were alignable.
evidence: This describes the success rate of the fiducial-less alignment method.

claim: It takes about 30 to 45 min to collect, process, and analyze a single tomogram.
source: It takes about 30 to 45 min to collect, process, and analyze a single tomogram.
evidence: This describes the total time required for the tomography workflow.

claim: Routine single particle grid and sample characterization by cryoET may increase microscope efficiency.
source: Thus, routine single particle grid and sample characterization by cryoET may not only provide information for optimizing grid preparation of a particular sample, but may also increase microscope efficiency.
evidence: This is inferred from the benefits demonstrated throughout the study.

claim: CryoET should be routinely performed on single particle cryoEM grids in order to fully understand the nature of the sample on the grid and to assist with the entire single particle collection and processing workflow.
source: We contend that cryoET should be routinely performed on single particle cryoEM grids in order to fully understand the nature of the sample on the grid and to assist with the entire single particle collection and processing workflow.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the findings of the study.

claim: A standalone Docker version of the Appion-Protomo fiducial-less tilt-series alignment suite is available at https://github.com/nysbc/appion-protomo.
source: We have made available a standalone Docker version of the Appion-Protomo fiducial-less tilt-series alignment suite used in these investigations at https://github.com/nysbc/appion-protomo.
evidence: This is stated as a resource made available by the authors.

claim: The observation that the vast majority of particles are adsorbed to air-water interfaces warrants further research into methods for avoiding the air-water interface.
source: The observation that the vast majority of particles are adsorbed to air-water interfaces warrants further research into methods for avoiding the air-water interface.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the main finding of the study.

claim: Possible methods for avoiding the air-water interface include preparing grids with non-ionic surfactants, using affinity grids, encapsulating particles in carbon layers, encapsulating particles in scaffolds, and faster plunging technologies.
source: Possible methods include preparing grids with non-ionic surfactants, using affinity grids, encapsulating particles in carbon layers, encapsulating particles in scaffolds, and, perhaps, faster plunging technologies to outrun air-water interface adsorption.
evidence: These are proposed solutions based on the findings and cited literature.

claim: Avoiding the air-water interface may prove critical for obtaining higher resolution structures of more fragile proteins.
source: Avoiding the air-water interface may prove critical for obtaining higher resolution structures of more fragile proteins.
evidence: This is speculated based on the findings about particle behavior at air-water interfaces.

claim: Increasing the concentration of bulk proteins in solution from 0.1 to 100 mg/mL results in an increased thickness of the denatured protein film at the air-water interface from 5 to 50 nm for β-casein.
source: Evidence from LB trough studies of the small, disordered protein β-casein additionally show that increasing the concentration of bulk proteins in solution from 0.1 to 100 mg/mL results in an increased thickness of the denatured protein film at the air-water interface from 5 to 50 nm (Meinders et al., 2001).
evidence: This is cited from Meinders et al., 2001.

claim: If particles are undergoing conformational change at either the protein-air-water interface or at the protein-protein network interface, then anomalous structures might be present after 2D and 3D classification that are practically indistinguishable from the nominal structures.
source: We speculate that if particles are undergoing conformational change at either the protein-air-water interface or at the protein-protein network interface, then anomalous structures might be present after 2D and 3D classification that are practically indistinguishable from the nominal structures.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed protein behavior and cited literature.

claim: Overlapping particles picked as one particle will need to be discarded during post-processing.
source: First, overlapping particles picked as one particle will need to be discarded during post-processing (particles not circled in Figure 7).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of overlapping particles and standard single particle processing practices.

claim: If overlapping particles are not discarded, then anomalous results might be expected in any 3D refinement containing these particles.
source: If these particles are not discarded, then anomalous results might be expected in any 3D refinement containing these particles – particularly in refinement models that use maximum likelihood methods such as Relion (Scheres, 2012), cryoSPARC (Punjani et al., 2017), and Xmipp (Scheres et al., 2007; Scheres et al., 2008) – thus reducing the reliability and accuracy of the refinement results.
evidence: This is inferred from understanding of single particle processing methods and the effects of overlapping particles.

claim: For an exposure area perpendicular to the electron beam containing two parallel layers of particles with identical concentrations, the whole-image defocus estimation will be located halfway-between the two layers.
source: For instance, an exposure area perpendicular to the electron beam containing two parallel layers of particles with identical concentrations will result in a whole-image defocus estimation located halfway-between the two layers, thus limiting the resolution of each particle depending on their distance from the midway point.
evidence: This is inferred from understanding of CTF estimation methods.

claim: For an image collected with a defocus range of 1 to 2 microns and with a 10 nm deviation from the midway point, the particles will have a resolution limit of about 2.5 Å.
source: For such an image collected with a defocus range of 1 to 2 microns and with a 10 nm deviation from the midway point, the particles will have a resolution limit of about 2.5 Å.
evidence: This is calculated based on CTF theory.

claim: A 50 nm deviation from the midway point will result in a resolution limit of about 6 Å.
source: A 50 nm deviation from the midway point will result in a resolution limit of about 6 Å.
evidence: This is calculated based on CTF theory.

claim: There is no apparent correlation between microscope and tilt direction or magnitude.
source: There is no apparent correlation between microscope and tilt direction or magnitude.
evidence: This is observed from the data in Table 2.

claim: Most of the particles listed in Tables 1 and 2 that have no apparent preferred orientations are adsorbed to the air-water interfaces.
source: Indeed, most of the particles listed in Tables 1 and 2 that have no apparent preferred orientations are adsorbed to the air-water interfaces.
evidence: This is observed from the data in Tables 1 and 2.

claim: Collection on a given grid with non-zero tilts effectively increases the number of imaged preferred orientations of the particle.
source: Collection on a given grid with non-zero tilts effectively increases the number of imaged preferred orientations of the particle.

claim: A preferentially oriented particle might have no apparent preferred orientations in a full single particle dataset depending on the numbers of preferred orientations, the locations of the preferred orientations on the particle, the symmetry of the particle, and the range of non-zero tilts on the grid.
source: Depending on the numbers N and/or M, the locations of the preferred orientations on the particle, the symmetry of the particle, and the range of non-zero tilts on the grid, a preferentially oriented particle might have no apparent preferred orientations in a full single particle dataset.

claim: For a micrograph with a single particle layer in the exposure area and a particle layer tilt of 10° collected at 1 Å pixelsize on a 4 k × 4 k camera with a defocus range of 1 to 2 microns, if the CTF is estimated and corrected on a whole-image basis, then the worst-corrected particles will have a resolution limit of around 4 Å.
source: As a hypothetical example, consider a micrograph with a single particle layer in the exposure area and a particle layer tilt of 10° collected at 1 Å pixelsize on a 4 k × 4 k camera with a defocus range of 1 to 2 microns. If the CTF for this micrograph is estimated and corrected for on a whole-image basis, then the worst-corrected particles will have a resolution limit of around 4 Å.
evidence: This is calculated based on CTF theory for the hypothetical example.

claim: Several samples show an asymmetry between particle saturation at the top and bottom air-water interfaces.
source: Several samples show an asymmetry between particle saturation at the top and bottom air-water interfaces.

claim: Samples #10, 12–15, 33, and 44 have particles covering one air-water interface with the other interface showing no particles.
source: For example, samples #10, 12–15, 33, and 44 have particles covering one air-water interface with the other interface showing no particles, samples #4, 7, 9, 18, 32, 36, 39, 42, and 43 have more particles covering one air-water interface than the other, and samples #1, 8, 9, 16, 17, 20–22, 24–31, 39, and 45 have a roughly equal number of particles on each air-water interface (Figure 6).
evidence: This is observed from the data in Tables 1 and 2.

claim: Particles that layer only on one air-water interface suggest that they are either sticking to the first available air-water interface or to the first-formed protein network film.
source: Particles that layer only on one air-water interface suggest that they are either sticking to the first available air-water interface (the interface on the back of the grid prior to blotting for conventional grid preparation techniques or the interface in the direction of application momentum for Spotiton), or to the first-formed protein network film.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed asymmetry and understanding of grid preparation processes.
